statement: By 31 October 2011, 128 deaths in the UK, Channel Islands and Isle of Man had been alleged to be associated with mephedrone. Tests after death found no mephedrone in 25 (19.5%, editors’ calculation), and 13 results were pending. The Results describe 90 as positive, 69 with concluded inquests, and 62 with forms received and analysed (Schifano et al., 2012). This flow has an exception: Table 2 says one of the 62 died in hospital three weeks after taking mephedrone and had none found after death. The paper mentions ante-mortem findings collectively but does not give this person’s individual confirmation evidence. A negative test after death does not establish no earlier exposure. The cases came from the National Programme on Substance Abuse Deaths, internet searches of toxicology and news sites, and a toxicology group. Coroners and Scottish procurators fiscal supplied records; media reports sometimes filled gaps. The register admits deaths with a directly implicated psychoactive substance, a history of dependence or misuse, or a controlled drug present after death. Presence of mephedrone itself could meet the last criterion only after its classification, which the paper dates to spring 2010; the entry criterion for each death is not stated (editors’ reading; Schifano et al., 2012). Mephedrone was the only substance identified in 8 of 62. The remaining 54 (62−8, editors’ calculation) were outside that only-substance group; this subtraction does not establish an individual co-detection result for the post-mortem-negative exception. Alcohol 26, other stimulants 22 and hypnotics or sedatives 22 were the most common other categories. Categories overlap and do not identify which substance caused a death. Mephedrone was formally named in the recorded cause in 36, on its own in 18. Who made those causal decisions and what evidence or rules they used are unstated (Schifano et al., 2012). The authors separately grouped 26 deaths as acute drug toxicity, 18 as self-inflicted harm, 6 as risky behaviour, 5 as collapse at a party, 5 as delayed hospital deaths and 2 as risky sexual activity. Those circumstance groups differ from the legal verdicts: 35 accident or misadventure, 11 suicide, 8 open, 5 drug misuse, and 1 each homicide, natural causes and narrative. The paper does not reconcile 18 self-inflicted deaths with 11 suicide verdicts; neither classification establishes that mephedrone caused self-harm (Schifano et al., 2012). The authors explicitly distinguish detection from causation and caution that failure to detect mephedrone may reflect test limitations. They regard the count as a minimum because some positive cases awaited inquest, geographical reporting was incomplete and tests varied. About 95% of coroners’ areas in England and Wales reported regularly; this is not 95% completeness of deaths across the UK. Untested or unalleged deaths could also be missed (editors’ inference, not a measured source finding). The Discussion names blood for the quantified levels, but blood type, sampling site and time, laboratory methods and panels are not described. With no count of use, this series supplies no death rate. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: How many deaths linked to mephedrone were confirmed? By October 2011, 128 deaths had been alleged in the UK and nearby islands. Tests after death found no mephedrone in 25, and 13 results were pending. Of 62 deaths analysed, mephedrone was the only substance found in 8. One person died weeks later in hospital and had none found after death; the paper does not explain their individual earlier test evidence. Being counted as confirmed did not mean mephedrone caused the death. The authors also say tests and reporting could miss deaths. This study cannot give a death rate.
magnitude: 128 alleged: 25 post-mortem-negative, 13 pending, 90 described as positive; 69 concluded inquests; 62 analysed, including the Table 2 post-mortem-negative exception. Editors’ calculations: 25/128=19.5%, 25/115 with results=21.7%, 8/62 only-substance=12.9%, 36/62 named-in-cause=58.1%, outside only-substance group 54=62−8 (not individual co-detection evidence for the negative exception). Named alone in recorded cause 18. Other substances: alcohol 26, stimulants 22, hypnotics/sedatives 22, opioids 13, piperazines 13, other cathinones 13. Author circumstance groups 26/18/6/5/5/2 differ from legal verdicts 35/11/8/5/1/1/1. No use denominator or printed intervals.

risk_of_bias.note: Allegation-based selection, incomplete reporting and concluded-inquest restriction; the Results’ positive-test definition has one Table 2 exception. The register’s presence criterion applies to controlled drugs, with mephedrone classification dated spring 2010. Blood is named broadly, but methods, sample type/site/timing and causal attribution rules are missing. Card sc_schifano_2012 retains high risk.

indirectness.note: Not downgraded: the claim is worded for the UK series it describes, 2009 to 2011.

imprecision.note: Small counts (8 deaths with mephedrone alone; 25 negative) without printed intervals, and no denominator.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS§6.3); retained downgrades for risk of bias and imprecision give very low. One UK/islands series: single-study and draft retained. It describes alleged and detected deaths separately from recorded causation; missing tests or allegations are editors’ possible undercount routes, not author-measured losses. A negative post-mortem finding does not exclude earlier exposure.

statement: Other drugs are often detected in deaths labelled heroin overdose, but detection does not establish which substances caused a death. A 1996 narrative review, with no stated search or appraisal, selected medical-examiner and coroner series and statistics from the USA, Australia and Europe, mostly published 1967–1996, leaning on the authors’ 152 deaths in New South Wales in 1992. It relays morphine as the only drug detected in 23%–48% across six series and alcohol in 29%–75% across 13, with mean blood alcohol 0.09–0.16 g/100 mL where reported. Diazepam alone was detected in 12% in one study; three others reported benzodiazepines in 22%, 27% and 55%. These are second-hand findings with unknown laboratory panels and varying death definitions, not shares proved to have been caused by heroin alone or by combinations (Darke & Zador, 1996). Five cited studies reported lower blood morphine when alcohol was detected. Correlations were weak where given: −0.14 in 505 alcohol-positive deaths and −0.28 in the authors’ series. A third of their series was below the laboratories’ 0.16 mg/L toxic level for people without opioid tolerance. A Michigan series published in 1977 reported 74% with morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died from other causes; the review does not establish its case-collection dates. It cites three survivor comparisons without numerical results and says better living-versus-fatal comparisons would add substantially to knowledge (Darke & Zador, 1996, second-hand). In the authors’ series 14% were classed as instant deaths and 22% took more than 3 hours; other series reported 44% beyond 2 hours and 52% beyond 3 hours. Other people were present in more than half of deaths in four studies (58%–79% where specified). The reviewers infer that combined drug toxicity explains many deaths. The editors’ limitation is that presence alone does not establish causal shares, tolerance was not measured, and delayed death is another possible explanation for low morphine. Darke and Zador do not discuss post-mortem redistribution; that separate limitation comes from toxicology literature, not their conclusions. The post-mortem result alone cannot decide the cause (Darke & Zador, 1996; Borra et al., 2026). In England and Wales in 2000, researchers reclassified1,037 accidental drug-related deaths voluntarily reported by coroners to a register of unstated completeness. They assigned 802 (77%) to direct overdose and 235 (23%) to other categories: 74 acute physical events, 112 toxicity with a medical condition, 31 traumatic accidents and 18 acute infections. Direct overdose was the default when no evidence suggested otherwise. Thus 77% is an upper bound for that default category and 23% a lower bound for alternatives under this record-based scheme—not a validated misclassification rate or a comparison with official statistics (editors’ reading; Webb et al., 2003). Heroin/morphine was recorded as implicated in 424 of 802 direct overdoses and detected in 488; it was implicated in 42 of 74 acute physical events, 33 of 72 deaths with a drug-related medical condition, and 11 of 18 infections. Alcohol was detected in 316 of 802 direct overdoses (39.4%), but the register recorded it only alongside other drugs. Methadone was implicated in 13% of direct overdoses, as the sole implicated drug in 4%; sole implication does not mean no other drug was detected. Negative findings were not recorded, leaving absence versus lack of testing uncertain (Webb et al., 2003). Heroin exposure can also be missed. A review reports falling femoral-blood 6-MAM, a heroin marker, between post-mortem samples in one primary study. It also relays both higher and lower post-mortem opioid concentrations compared with samples from life, with additional timing, specimen and morphine-transformation limits (Borra et al., 2026). Another review’s table says cerebrospinal-fluid 6-MAM detected 46% more heroin-related cases than blood, but supplies no case counts or unique per-value primary citation; this is a second-hand testing comparison, not 46% more proven heroin-caused deaths (Leikin & Watson, 2003). The main death-series figures are historical and cannot describe current drug mixtures or yield a rate per use. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Are deaths labelled heroin overdose always caused by heroin alone? Other drugs were often found in the older studies, but that does not show which caused a death. A review relays morphine as the only drug found in 23 to 48 in 100 deaths, and alcohol in 29 to 75 in 100. Diazepam-only and whole-group benzodiazepine figures measure different things. In England and Wales in 2000, at least 23 in 100 reported accidental drug-related deaths were put in categories beyond direct overdose, using the researchers’ rules. Other drugs or illnesses may matter, and heroin exposure may also be missed by tests. These records cannot tell how many deaths heroin alone caused.
magnitude: Secondary review: morphine-only 23%–48% across 6 series; alcohol 29%–75% across 13, mean 0.09–0.16 g/100 mL; diazepam-only 12% in 1, benzodiazepines 22%, 27%, 55% in 3 others. Correlations −0.14 in 505 alcohol-positive deaths and −0.28. One series: a third below 0.16 mg/L, instant 14%, over 3 h 22%; other series over 2 h 44%, over 3 h 52%; others present 58%–79%. Michigan paper published 1977: 74% no higher than comparison deaths. England/Wales 2000: 1,037; default direct-overdose 802/1,037=77.3% ceiling and alternatives 235/1,037=22.7% floor under that scheme (editors calculations), not official-statistics error estimates. Heroin/morphine implicated 424/802, detected 488/802; implicated 42/74 acute events, 33/72 drug-related conditions, 11/18 infections. Alcohol co-detected 316/802=39.4%; methadone implicated 101/802≈13%, sole implicated 4%. CSF comparison 46% more heroin-related cases, secondary and without counts; not deaths proved caused by heroin.

risk_of_bias.note: The review chooses its studies without a stated search, leans on the authors' own series and does not appraise any study; laboratory panels and case definitions are unknown (card sc_darke_1996, editors' checklist high). The register is voluntary with unstated coverage, and its categories are the researchers' unvalidated reading of coroners' returns (phi 0.77 overall; card sc_webb_2003, JBI high).

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: the shares vary widely between studies, as expected from different panels, places and decades, but all point the same way (other drugs are often present in deaths attributed to heroin).

indirectness.note: Retained one-level downgrade: most death-series figures are secondary reports from publications 1967–1996 or one England/Wales register year 2000; they cannot describe present-day drug mixtures. No assumption that fentanyl was absent from every older series is needed.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded: the claim gives ranges across studies, not a single estimate.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS§6.3); unchanged risk-of-bias and indirectness downgrades give very low. Replicated describes repeated co-detection/alternative mechanisms across historical series and a separate register, not replication of a causal share. The same primary series relayed by a review is counted once. Sole detection, sole implication and causal attribution remain distinct. Draft retained.

statement: These studies do not establish a blood-MDMA cutoff that separates death caused by MDMA from other deaths or survival. They show overlap, while differing in population, specimen and sampling time. A Sheffield department reviewed 77 autopsies with MDMA or related compounds detected in 1992–2008. Of the full series, 17 deaths were attributed principally to MDMA, 30 to several drugs and 28 to trauma, with 2 other deaths. The blood-value subsets were 13, 22 and 24 respectively. Femoral-blood MDMA ranged 0.478–53.9 mg/L (median 3.49), 0.04–41.5 (median 0.76) and 0.035–4.81 (median 0.483). The toxicity median was about 7.2 times the trauma median; at least 7 of 13 toxicity values fall within the trauma range (editors’ calculations from the order statistics and ranges, not individual data; Milroy, 2011). The author concludes that concentration needs the history and full autopsy findings. He treats trauma deaths as a proxy for ordinary-use levels, but no living ordinary-use group was measured and MDMA could have contributed to a collision, fall or drowning. Certifiers, attribution rules and their knowledge of concentrations are not reported. If high levels influenced classification, the observed separation could partly reflect that decision; this is the editors’ possible-bias explanation, not Milroy’s documented method. He also notes possible low levels after water intoxication through dilution (Milroy, 2011). A striking specimen comparison cited by Milroy belongs to Elliott’s separate study of deaths after hospital admission, not the Sheffield 77. In one case sampled 2 days after death, heart blood 28.39 mg/L was about 3.9–4.6 times the two femoral values 6.19 and 7.25; an earlier serum value 4.33 had been taken a day before death. These are second-hand values from different sites, times and matrices, not an isolated measure of redistribution (Milroy, 2011, reporting Elliott). Henry et al. reported 7 deaths aged 16–21 among London poisons-service enquiries in 1990–1991. Recorded temperatures were 40–43°C; plasma MDMA was 0.11–1.26 mg/L in 5 quantified fatal cases, with sampling times unstated. The paper also gives 8 survivor values: 5 after severe complications (including a child’s accidental exposure) and 3 after road accidents. Together they ranged 0.05–0.97 mg/L and overlapped the fatal range; all 5 severe-case values lay inside it (editors’ comparison of Tables I–III). These are selected hospital plasma measurements, not post-mortem femoral blood or healthy ordinary use. The separate 7.72 mg/L case has only a short description of hangover, tachycardia and hypertension, with sampling time and detailed follow-up unstated; it cannot define a tolerated range (Henry et al., 1992). A previously checked Finnish source extraction records 57 medico-legal autopsies of all causes with MDMA in femoral blood in 2000–2010, median 0.30 mg/L and 97.5th percentile 4.0; its table prints 0% fatal poisoning with MDMA as the main finding (Launiainen & Ojanperä, 2014; primary full text unavailable in this continuation). That category excludes other possible contributions. With 57 cases, one would round to 2%, so ordinary whole-percent rounding is consistent with none in that specific category (editors’ arithmetic), not proof of no MDMA contribution. A narrative review relays one published lethal-MDMA range of 40–8,500 µg/L, equivalent to 0.04–8.5 mg/L (Ferner, 2008, second-hand). Borra et al. report higher femoral MDMA after death than earlier plasma or serum, without effect sizes; elimination before death, incomplete absorption or distribution, possible later administration, hospital selection and specimen differences prevent attributing each difference solely to redistribution (2026). None of these findings supplies a validated ordinary-use comparison or fatal cutoff. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: What blood level of MDMA is fatal? These studies do not establish a cutoff. In Sheffield, levels in deaths attributed to MDMA overlapped with levels in people who died of injuries. In the London paper, hospital plasma levels in 8 survivors also overlapped the 5 measured fatal cases. Some survivors had been severely ill; these were not healthy people after ordinary use. Hospital plasma and blood taken at autopsy are different comparisons, and sampling times were often unknown. The Finnish table concerns poisoning mainly attributed to MDMA, not every possible contribution. A concentration needs the rest of the case evidence.
magnitude: Sheffield 1992–2008: 77 autopsies, full-category totals 17 MDMA/30 polydrug/28 trauma/2 other; blood subsets 13/22/24. Femoral-blood ranges (mg/L)/medians: 0.478–53.9/3.49; 0.04–41.5/0.76; 0.035–4.81/0.483. Editors calculation: median ratio 7.2, at least 7 of 13 toxicity values within trauma range. Henry 1990–1991: 7 deaths, 5 quantified plasma 0.11–1.26 mg/L; 8 survivor values 0.05–0.97, including 5 severe-complication survivors all within fatal range. Brief separate 7.72 case has limited clinical/timing data. External Elliott case via Milroy: heart/femoral ratio 3.9–4.6, not Sheffield. Inherited Finnish 57 cases, median 0.30, 97.5th percentile 4.0 mg/L, 0% fatal poisoning with MDMA main finding; 1/57=1.75%≈2% if rounded (editors calculation). Ferner secondary range 40–8,500 µg/L=0.04–8.5 mg/L. No individual prediction or use denominator.

risk_of_bias.note: Unstated certifiers, attribution rules and knowledge of concentrations; possible incorporation bias is conditional. Trauma is an assumed ordinary-use proxy, not a measured living group. Henry is a selected poisons-service series with hospital plasma and unstated sampling times; the extreme survivor has limited detail. Both cards retain high risk.

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: all sources point to overlap and none supports a threshold.

indirectness.note: No living ordinary-use comparison. Henry supplies 8 selected survivors, including severe illness and accidents; plasma is not post-mortem whole femoral blood. Different survival/sampling intervals and historical populations limit cross-study comparisons.

imprecision.note: Small Sheffield blood subsets 13/22/24 without individual values; Henry 5 quantified fatal cases and 8 survivors, plus a briefly described extreme case; Finnish 57 from an inherited checked extraction whose primary is unavailable here.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive evidence starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS§6.3); unchanged downgrades for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision reach very low. Replicated refers to independent Sheffield and London overlap findings, not a validated universal threshold. The Finnish registry provides a separate attribution distribution rather than proof of survivor overlap; its primary was not freshly verified. Secondary series summarized by Milroy are not counted again. No advice on amounts, tablets or combinations; draft retained.

statement: Excited delirium is a disputed label for extreme agitation, sometimes with stimulant drugs present. The two reviews considered here do not establish whether the described state kills independently of restraint, or how much deaths given the label were caused by restraint, drugs or both. They report no validated diagnostic criteria or specific autopsy/laboratory marker, and discuss the label as a diagnosis of exclusion (Strömmer et al., 2020; Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026). The 2020 review says forensic-pathology publications almost exclusively use excited delirium and describe fatal cases, while clinical publications use both excited and agitated delirium for survivors as well as deaths. This describes source types, not a count of which professionals apply the label. The 2026 review also describes a checklist used with living people in policing and prehospital care. It favours acute behavioral disturbance, retains the older term when citing its sources, and recommends replacement where possible; Strömmer’s team instead proposes agitated delirium with a modifier for restraint and a homicide or undetermined manner in restrained fatal cases. These are the authors’ recommendations, not conclusions tested by the data. Strömmer’s pooled analysis selected 168 individually described cases from 61 English-language reports/series found to 23 April 2020. Of 120 labelled excited delirium, 92 died; of 48 labelled agitated delirium, 12 died (unadjusted odds ratio 9.9). Some force was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths and 43 of 64 survivors; none in 2 deaths and 1 survivor, and unknown in 8 deaths and 20 survivors. Force covers manual actions, handcuffs, hog/hobble ties, electrical weapons, sedation and other measures; it does not mean every case involved prone compression. These categories overlap. Cocaine was noted in 55 of 104 deaths and 19 of 64 survivors, as classified from case reports without standardized toxicology assessment or drug concentrations (Strömmer et al., 2020). The authors argue that restraint and the label are intertwined, and find no reliable evidence for an independent lethal syndrome. Their own limitations acknowledge nonrandom publication, overrepresentation and better documentation of deaths, and missing drug and restraint details. The editors’ appraisal is that source type, selection and clustering can connect the label, death and recorded force; the univariate analysis does not adjust for them. Only 3 cases explicitly had no force, and 28 had force status unknown, so neither absence of an independently lethal condition nor a causal death risk from restraint can be established. Some printed tables are internally inconsistent: Table 4 gives 100% mortality to a cited study whose title specifies non-fatal encounters. No corrected group fatality rate is supplied here; the later exchange is not part of the 2020 source (Strömmer et al., 2020). The 2026 narrative systematic review searched 2010–2025 and describes cocaine, methamphetamine and phencyclidine as frequently detected, without proportions or concentrations. It favours ventilatory compromise with metabolic collapse during prone restraint, but also allows stress/stimulant-associated arrhythmia in some deaths. It also cites case reports of deaths attributed to excited delirium without overt restraint. Attribution in those reports is not proof that the state itself caused death; the primary reports were not read. It describes volunteer experiments without clinically significant hypoxia or major circulatory compromise, and low mortality in some operational cohorts, while explaining why these do not reproduce all real-world conditions (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026, secondary summaries). For certification and counting, the 2026 review cites 46 Ontario investigation reports with most deaths classified accidental or natural and reports undercounting of restraint-related deaths without quantifying it. Its sources and methods are heterogeneous; the complete included-study set and supplement are unavailable here. The two reviews are rated critically low and overlap because the 2026 review cites Strömmer. They cannot quantify drug-caused deaths or give a causal verdict for an individual. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: What is excited delirium, and why is it disputed? It is a label for extreme agitation, used with living people as well as after deaths. These reviews report no agreed validated criteria or specific autopsy sign. In 168 published cases, force was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths, but force included sedation and electrical weapons as well as being held down. Only 3 cases explicitly had no force; many had missing information. A later review also cites deaths attributed to the label without overt restraint. That does not prove what caused them. The selected reports cannot show how often restraint, drugs or the agitated state caused death. See the contested question.
magnitude: Selected individually described cases: 168 from 61 reports; 104 deaths, 64 survivors; excited 92/120 fatal versus agitated 12/48, unadjusted OR 9.9. Force: 94/104 deaths versus 43/64 survivors (editors subtraction from Table 2 none/unknown); none 2/1, unknown 8/20; total explicitly none 3, unknown 28. Police first 95/120 versus 16/48; handcuffs 80/120 versus 6/48; hog/hobble 46/120 versus 1/48. Cocaine noted 55/104 versus 19/64. These are selected-report associations, not causal effects or encounter rates. Secondary 2026 review: Finland 12/21,036 autopsies=0.06%; 229 deaths, 58% collapse within 1–5 min, at least 20% respiratory distress; Ontario 46 reports, most accidental/natural. No frequency of causal drug contribution. 2020 grouped rates are not repaired from unavailable later exchange.

risk_of_bias.note: Both reviews retain critically-low appraisals. Pooled cases are selected for publication; source type, case clustering, label and recording differ; analysis is univariate and several printed tables are inconsistent. The 2026 review does not identify the complete included set in its main article; primary studies and reviews may overlap, and a cited rapid-collapse source concerns litigation. Later exchange full texts and 2026 supplement are unavailable here.

inconsistency.note: The two reviews, and the evidence within them, are read in opposite ways: deaths labelled 'excited delirium' as restraint deaths, or as deaths from an agitated state and stimulant drugs in which restraint is incidental.

indirectness.note: Selected case/death reports are not a sample of all severe-agitation encounters. Clinical papers include both survivors and deaths. Force categories combine different actions and sedation; drug categories are taken from case descriptions without standardized concentrations. Volunteer data do not reproduce every real-world custodial circumstance.

imprecision.note: Only 3 pooled cases explicitly record no force, while 28 are unknown; no denominator of all encounters or count of causally drug-involved deaths. The 2 no-force deaths do not establish a mechanism.

publication_bias.note: Not separately rated; selection for publication is covered under risk of bias.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; unchanged two-level risk-of-bias and one-level inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision downgrades reach the very-low floor. Status remains contested with all six debate fields. The 2026 review cites Strömmer, so they are not independent replication. Authors’ terminology recommendations differ; the newer review retains the old term for source fidelity and says replace where possible. Professional-body positions, primary no-restraint cases and later exchange content are not independently verified here. Draft retained.
